assessment.security_status_cs: Situace v Rudém moři a oblasti Perského zálivu zůstává extrémně napjatá kvůli pokračujícím útokům Houthiů na saúdská letiště a ropná zařízení. Blokáda Hormuzského průlivu spolu s novými sankcemi vůči íránské stínové flotile žene ceny námořní přepravy a ropy prudce vzhůru.
assessment.security_status_en: The situation in the Red Sea and Persian Gulf remains extremely tense due to ongoing Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and oil infrastructure. The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with new sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet, is driving maritime freight rates and oil prices sharply upward.

recommendations.reason_cs: Rekordní poplatky za supertankery a nutnost vyhýbat se nebezpečným koridorům výrazně zvyšují marže přepravců. Geopolitická rizika udržují sazby na vysokých úrovních.
recommendations.reason_en: Record supertanker fees and the necessity to avoid dangerous corridors significantly boost carriers' margins. Geopolitical risks keep freight rates at elevated levels.

recommendations.sector_cs: Obranný průmysl (např. RTX, Lockheed Martin, BAE Systems)

recommendations.reason_cs: Escalace konfliktu na Blízkém východě a útoky na kritickou infrastrukturu zvyšují poptávku po protivzdušné obraně a vojenském vybavení. Vládní výdaje na obranu v regionu i globálně porostou.
recommendations.reason_en: Escalation in the Middle East and attacks on critical infrastructure drive demand for air defense and military equipment. Government defense spending in the region and globally will increase.

recommendations.sector_cs: Ropa a Plyn (např. Shell, BP, Chevron)

recommendations.reason_en: Brent crude holds above $100 due to threats in the Strait of Hormuz and low EU gas storage levels. Major oil companies benefit from high commodity margins.

recommendations.sector_cs: Evropský Spotřební sektor & Autoprůmysl (např. Volvo, BMW)
recommendations.reason_cs: Rostoucí náklady na dopravu, drahá energetická aktiva a sociální nepokoje v Evropě negativně dopadají na marže a spotřebitelskou poptávku. Inflační tlaky se vracejí.
recommendations.reason_en: Rising transport costs, expensive energy assets, and social unrest in Europe negatively impact margins and consumer demand. Inflationary pressures are returning.

recommendations.sector_cs: Pražská burza: ČEZ, Komerční banka, Erste Group
recommendations.sector_en: Prague Stock Exchange: ČEZ, Komerční banka, Erste Group
recommendations.reason_cs: Domácí banky a energetika čelí celoevropskému tlaku na růst nákladů a nejistotě ohledně ekonomického výhledu EU. Valuace jsou sice stabilní, ale chybí silné růstové impulzy.
recommendations.reason_en: Domestic banks and utilities face pan-European cost pressures and uncertainty regarding the EU economic outlook. Valuations are stable, but strong growth catalysts are lacking.

recommendations.sector_cs: Evropské blue-chips (např. Airbus, TotalEnergies, Allianz, Rheinmetall)
recommendations.sector_en: European blue-chips (e.g. Airbus, TotalEnergies, Allianz, Rheinmetall)
recommendations.reason_cs: Zatímco energetické a zbrojní tituly profitují z krize, zbytek evropského trhu čelí brzdícímu růstu a energetické krizi. Diverzifikované portfolia vyžadují selektivní přístup.
recommendations.reason_en: While energy and defense titles profit from the crisis, the rest of the European market faces slowing growth and an energy crunch. Diversified portfolios require a selective approach.

assessment.forecast_cs: V nejbližších dnech lze očekávat další eskalaci napětí v regionu Perského zálivu a Rudého moře, což udrží ceny ropy nad hranicí 100 USD za barel. Logistické trasy zůstanou vysoce rizikové s dopadem na globální dodavatelské řetězce.
assessment.forecast_en: Over the coming days, further escalation of tensions in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea is expected, keeping oil prices above the $100 per barrel mark. Logistics routes will remain high-risk, impacting global supply chains.
assessment.forecast_review_cs: Předchozí předpověď se plně potvrdila, jelikož nedávné útoky na saúdská letiště a narušení dopravy v Hormuzském průlivu udržely vysokou volatilitu a napětí na trhu s komoditami.
assessment.forecast_review_en: The previous forecast was fully confirmed, as recent attacks on Saudi airports and transport disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz maintained high volatility and market tension in commodities.

articles.title: Why this is no disaster for Polanski: Greens remain competitive as voters reward Burnham
articles.summary:
Why this is no disaster for Polanski: Greens remain competitive as voters reward Burnham

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Fri, 10/09/2026 - 10:21
The Green vote share surged to a historic high in Holborn and St Pancras, despite the party leader losing to Labour
Green Party leader Zack Polanski reacts following the results in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, triggered by the resignation of Keir Starmer as MP, 9 October (Reuters/Toby Shepheard)
Off

Is this the end of Zack Polanski as leader of the Green Party? Many seem to think so - indeed, multiple national newspapers have suggested it.

No doubt there are people in his party who want him out now he’s failed to be elected to parliament for Holborn and St Pancras.

But on closer examination, Polanski’s defeat on Friday morning is far less of a catastrophe than many of his critics are claiming.

The Green vote share surged to a historic high in the seat, and with a volatile electorate there are clear signs that the party can be optimistic about its potential for future growth.

This is undeniably a victory for Andy Burnham. Labour’s candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali - with one of the most unusual backstories in British politics, as a child refugee from Somalia who enjoyed enormous success in local politics and rose to become leader of Camden Council - is locally well-known and popular.

Ironically, Abdi-Wali is an ally of Keir Starmer, who she will replace in parliament, and her political positions have often seemed closer to Starmer’s than the new prime minister’s.

Yet there’s little doubt that her win is in no small part a reflection of the "Burnham bounce" in the national polls. 

'We're waiting to sweep up their votes': Three days inside the Green Party conference
Read More »

In the ethnically diverse Holborn and St Pancras, where the Gaza genocide remains a salient issue, many voters will have almost certainly wanted to reward the Burnham government for its recent sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements.

Many voters, meanwhile, will simply be relieved that Starmer is gone and replaced by a more personable figure. 

Burnham is showing Labour can defend its seats and is clawing back votes it lost under Starmer. 

But this by-election won’t particularly embolden Labour strategists who are mulling an early general election next spring.

The Green Party gave Labour a serious run for its money, with Polanski winning 8,928 votes (32.8 percent) to Abdi-Wali’s 12,292 (45.2 percent).

Labour’s majority, just 3,364 votes, is extremely slim. By comparison Starmer’s majority was 11,572 votes in the 2024 general election, and even then his had been significantly slashed by independent candidate Andrew Feinstein. 

Remember that Holborn and St Pancras is historically a Labour stronghold. That status quo hasn’t exactly returned. 

Polanski has changed the party's fortunes

Many in the Green Party see Polanski’s decision to stand for election during Burnham’s honeymoon phase as a significant miscalculation. 

In the short term this by-election will likely deal a heavy blow to the party’s momentum and image. 

But look at what the Greens have achieved in the past year.

The party surged in the polls late last year after Polanski was elected leader. The Greens gained further momentum and credibility with a by-election victory in Gorton and Denton in February and then took more votes from Labour in the May local elections than Reform did.

'It’s a setback, not doom. We are the biggest threat to the establishment'

- Asma Alam, Green councillor

Polanski is at least partially responsible for Starmer's downfall and Burnham's premiership. This means the Greens are now suffering from their own success.

The party’s polling nationally has plummeted and is close to where it was in 2024. Crucially, however, in target seats - like London's Holborn and St Pancras - it is still performing strongly. 

It was never likely that Polanski could replicate the historic victory in Gorton and Denton, which mobilised both huge anti-Starmer sentiment and opposition to the visceral local threat of Reform. 

Yet Friday's was still the Green Party’s second best by-election result ever. Polanski has indisputedly changed the party’s fortunes. 

Hostile media

“The result is really sad, but we always knew this was going to be a tight battle,” Asma Alam, a Green councillor and campaign coordinator, told Middle East Eye on Friday morning.

“All this noise about new leadership needed is rubbish,” she added. “Zack won the leadership by a significant majority - that won’t change. 

“It’s a setback, not doom. We are the biggest threat to the establishment.”

Co-deputy leader Mothin Ali told MEE at the party’s conference last weekend that "what we can continue to do is make sure that we’re holding the government to account".

Ali added that if the Greens "are continuously providing better alternatives, the Labour government is going to have to take notice.

"And if they don't, then we're waiting to sweep up their votes."

The Greens have much to reflect on, including how the party can effectively deal with hostile media coverage, which will only increase. 

The by-election came after days of vociferous attacks on the Greens in the national media over the party conference vote last weekend to declare Zionism a form of racism. 

There is no evidence that anger over the conference vote played a role in influencing the by-election, but it is nonetheless likely that the barrage of hostile media coverage of Polanski and the Greens will have put off some undecided voters.

Everything to play for

Significantly, the "Zionism is racism" motion, which dominated media coverage of the conference, involved Green activists, not the leadership, shaping the agenda.

Polanski wasn’t even at the conference for the vote itself - he expressed discomfort with elements of the motion, although he said he thinks Zionism is racist - because he was campaigning in Holborn. 

Green Party recognises Zionism as a form of racism and backs single Palestinian state
Read More »

“I refute the idea that the motion impacted the results,” Alam said. “What it lost in potential votes it also added in votes from people who preferred our strong stance.”

But Caroline Lucas, a former Green leader, has heaped criticism on Polanski, suggesting he failed to show leadership on the issue of the Zionism motion, which she strongly opposed.

Will the Greens now seek to change the party’s internal system to give the leadership more control over the formulation of policy? This may be necessary for the party’s growth, but it would trigger a revolt among the membership. 

Internally, the Greens have tough questions which they need to resolve.

Ultimately, though, the key lesson from Polanski’s performance in Holborn and St Pancras is that the electorate is still volatile.

Since the 2024 election we have seen the implosion of the two-party political system. With Burnham in power, many pundits have prophesied its return. 

This has not happened yet, as the close competition in the by-election indicates. Depending on the Burnham government’s performance, support for the Greens could either plummet further or surge again. Voters are less loyal than they once were and no party can take them for granted.

For both Labour and the Greens, then, there's everything to play for.

articles.title: 'No one listens to us': France's mass student protests expose social and racial inequality
articles.summary:
'No one listens to us': France's mass student protests expose social and racial inequality

Submitted by Pauline Ertel on Thu, 10/08/2026 - 01:02
Students from disadvantaged suburbs demand better conditions and equal opportunities in a system that has neglected their communities
Protesters during a blockade of Sciences Po university in Paris as part of nationwide protests demanding better school conditions in France, 7 October 2026 (Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters)
Off

As France's student protests stretch into a third week, testimonies from young people show how unequal and often degrading school conditions fall hardest on ethnic minorities and working‑class suburbs.

Police violence has intensified and schools have been disrupted nationwide, pushing students from the banlieues – France’s working‑class, often ethnically diverse suburbs – to demand better conditions and an end to the structural inequalities they say marginalise their communities.

The protests began in mid-September following a staff and students strike over teacher shortages and deteriorating conditions at the Lycee Saint-Exupery in Creteil, in the southeastern suburb of Paris. 

When videos of the strike circulated online, other high schools joined in, blocking entrances and staging demonstrations. Within 10 days, the movement had spread nationwide.

According to figures from the interior ministry, by 6 October around 250,000 people - including school and university students, parents, teachers and unionists - had taken to the streets to demand higher public investment in education and improved conditions, particularly in low‑income neighbourhoods.

Their demands range from renovated facilities and increased staffing to smaller class sizes, a fairer college application system and an alternative to the current “8h-18h” school day.

The French state has reacted with what rights groups, including Amnesty International, have condemned as an "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force, urging authorities to de-escalate.

Footage circulating online shows police and national guard units deploying tear gas, firing rubber bullets and beating protesters with batons. Hundreds have been injured, some very seriously.

In Val‑d’Oise, a 14‑year‑old lost several teeth after a tear‑gas canister was fired at his face at point‑blank range. In Lens, a 15-year old student lost his hand in a confrontation with police. Following the incident, the interior minister announced a temporary halt on stun grenades at school demonstrations, while rejecting accusations of police brutality.

Meanwhile, more than 5,000 protestors have been arrested - 85 percent of them minors, according to the ministry.

Dilapidated schools

The wave of high‑school blockades across the country has exposed a deep crisis in the education system. Material conditions are a central grievance.

In many high schools, particularly in low‑income areas, buildings are in severe disrepair. Students speak of leaks, damaged ceilings, rats, broken toilets, insufficient furniture, and classrooms which overheat during recent heatwaves.

'It's either freezing in the winter or unbearably hot in the summer. The power cuts out, so the classrooms go dark, the computers stop working, the lights stop working'

- Madeleine, high school student

Class sizes are often overcrowded, reaching more than 36 students in urban areas, and school days are notoriously long. On top of this, around 10 percent of teaching hours go undelivered, with teacher absences hitting poorer areas hardest.

"We have asbestos in the walls, classrooms where there aren’t enough chairs or desks. There are 35 of us in a classroom. We go to school from 8am to 6pm and then we have to do homework, it's impossible," a student from the Lycee Alfred Kastler in Pontoise, 30km northwest of Paris, told Middle East Eye. 

Other students criticised the lack of ventilation or air conditioning systems at school to battle surging heatwaves as well as repeated power failures.

"We have major problems with insulation. It's either freezing in the winter or unbearably hot in the summer," Madeleine, a student at the Lycee Francois Villon in Les Mureaux, 40km northweast of Paris, told MEE. 

"The power cuts out, so the classrooms go dark, the computers stop working, the lights stop working. Nothing works anymore." 

Ousmane, 17, from the Lycee Emily Bronte in Lognes, an eastern suburb of Paris, said some classrooms don’t even have chairs.

"Sometimes we have to stand during lessons," he told MEE.

Other students mentioned the state of sanitary facilities in schools, saying that bathrooms are not cleaned, and reporting a lack of toilet paper and soap. 

In response to the protests, the government has acknowledged the "legitimate" nature of the grievances and pledged to address class sizes, daily schedules, teacher replacement mechanisms and building conditions. According to a Senate report, billions of euros will be needed in the coming years to renovate thousands of ageing schools.  

Banlieues suffer disproportionately 

While underfunding affects schools across France, those in deprived neighbourhoods with large immigrant populations are hit hardest.

Unlike cities such as London, where different social and income groups as well has housing tenures are integrated within a single neighbourhood, Paris exposes a stark geographical divide, where wealth is heavily concentrated in the west and adjacent suburbs, while lower-income populations mainly live in peripheral northern and eastern banlieues. 

Criminalising protest: Pro-Palestine students in France face increased repression
Read More »

This contrast shapes students' experiences. According to the OECD, social background remains one of the strongest predictors of academic success, with disadvantaged pupils concentrated in under‑resourced schools where teacher absenteeism is higher and learning conditions poorer.

Jelan Kone, a student from the Lycee Paul Eluard, one of the first high schools to have joined the protest movement, in the northern suburb of Saint-Denis, told MEE that racialised prejudices towards disadvantaged cities and their populations perpetuate institutional neglect.

"They assume that because we’re from the banlieues, we’re supposed to be uneducated, that we don’t learn anything, that the suburbs are worthless," she told MEE.

"But we don’t just let people walk all over us. We try to improve our communities and show that the banlieues aren’t something that should be neglected," she added.

Mohamed, 17, who attends the selective Lycee International de L’Est Parisien in Noisy‑le‑Grand - one of the most disadvantaged cities in the Paris region, where 18.7 percent of residents live below the poverty threshold - stressed the importance of students from better‑resourced schools joining the movement.

"It’s sad that others don’t have the opportunity to improve their social situation. It’s very important for us, in this area, to support neighbouring high‑school students out of solidarity," he told MEE at a mass protest in Paris’s Place de la Republique on Tuesday.

'They assume that because we’re from the banlieues, we’re supposed to be uneducated, that the banlieues are worthless'

- Jelan, High school student 

Discrimination is also visible in the way police treat protesters, according to witness testimonies and extensive documentation of racial bias within French police forces.

A 2025 study by the independent administrative authority Défenseur des droits (Rights Defender) found that young men perceived as Black, Arab or North African face a risk of identity checks four times higher than other population groups.

Nellie, a high school student from the Lycee Alfred Kastler in the northwestern suburb of Cergy, told MEE police disproportionately target Black and Arab youth.

"During one of the school blockades, I heard one student say to a policeman: 'I don't speak to cops'. The police man replied: 'We don't speak to Black people'," she said.

Nellie's classmate Maelie told MEE that the police would "show up at their school, hit and tear-gas innocent people". 

'No one listens to us' 

Another source of frustration among students is Parcoursup, France’s national higher‑education application platform.

Students have raised concern over algorithmic biases in the system, saying that applicants from schools in more affluent neighbourhoods get prioritised, perpetuating already existing social and racial inequality. 

France: When racism peaks - and the mountains are claimed as white‑only spaces
Read More »

"We’re at a high school in the Paris banlieue. Because of that, we’re not viewed as favourably and it means that we don’t necessarily have the same opportunities as students from rich schools, even though we have the same level, and sometimes an even higher level than them," Imene, a high-school student in Saint-Denis, told MEE. 

"Parcoursup is a source of stress for all students in France. It’s unbearable. There are people who have an average grade of 18 out of 20 but were rejected by top universities, or from programmes like medicine, simply because other students were given priority," she added. 

Earlier this year, a Defenseur des droits report on discrimination based on origin among young people highlighted persistent inequalities in access to higher education and raised concerns about selection procedures, including Parcoursup.

It called for stronger measures to ensure equal treatment and issued recommendations for Parcoursup to publish clear, verifiable and understandable selection criteria, strengthen ministerial oversight of admissions algorithms, and prohibit the use of applicants’ previous high schools as a selection criterion.

Yet despite these calls for reform, many students say they still feel overlooked. Melissa, another high school student in Saint-Denis, told MEE that she feels that students, especially from the banlieues, are ignored by the government.  

"Everyone is equal in this country, we want to have the same rights as everyone else. That’s what they don’t want to understand. They just want us to stay quiet and put up with it," she said.

'We're not viewed as favorably and it means that we don't necessarily have the same opportunities as students from rich schools'

- Imene, high school student

Although many teachers support the protests, Imene, Melissa and Zara expressed concern over the socioeconomic gap between staff and pupils in Saint-Denis, which prevents them from relating to the students' grievances. 

"Most of our teachers studied at really prestigious universities. So for them, it’s not really the same experience. They don't come from the Paris banlieues, and they’re not racialised people," Imene told MEE.

The protest movement, they said, will continue until the "students will be heard", arguing that students and staff have raised these issues for years without meaningful change.

"Every single year, there’s another issue. But nothing changes," Zara said, deploring that despite the recurrent protests over the years, "no one listens to us".

While speaking to MEE, Zara, Imene and Melissa were preparing for another blockade of their school on the following day, painting slogans on cardboards. More and more students joined them. Despite the violence and uncertainty, they expressed determination - and hope.

"If we don’t act now, it’s never, ever, ever going to change. But this time, if we keep going, things will change, I have hope," Imene said. 

France

articles.title: Hegseth promises execution live stream as Trump appears to ‘pause’ war on Iran | First Thing
articles.summary:
US president says US will not attack Iran before midterms, while defense secretary says Nidal Hasan will face a firing squad next month. Plus, Sofia Coppola looks back on her glittering directorial career

Good morning. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has said the execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad will be livestreamed next month, in a radical departure from the previous norm. Hegseth said: “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center at Fort Hood, Texas, on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013 and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was in November 1945.

Why is Hegseth being criticised over the Iran war? The Democratic senator Chris Murphy said Hegseth was “determined to hide the cost and the consequences of this war from the American public”. Murphy claimed the Pentagon blocked him from visiting a military base in Qatar and that an Iranian strike on the US embassy in Riyadh was far worse than the public were led to believe.

What has Donald Trump said about the US war on Iran? The US president has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections, outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months. A Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September found that only about a third of Americans approved of the strikes on Iran.

Why are some voters calling Missouri’s elections ‘dizzying and embarrassing’? Thanks to a protracted legal battle over an effort by Republicans to redraw the state’s congressional map, some voters are no longer sure which congressional district they live in or who will be on their ballot paper for the midterms.

What happened in last night’s crucial midterm debates? Rachel Leingang, George Chidi and Auzzy Byrdsell have rounded up the key takeaways from debates in the battleground states of Michigan, Georgia and Maine.
